meaning: Boundlessness, inexhaustible abundance, unimpaired perfection, creative power — 'Infinity', one of the most ancient of the Indian goddesses and the mother of the Ādityas.

phonemes.desc: The a is the shwa of “about” — the prefix of negation.
From a-diti: “un-bound”, “un-fettered” — the name is a definition.
The feminine abstract ending, as in kīrti “fame” and śakti “power”: the quality itself made divine.

pronunciation.note: Her name is a sentence: she is “Boundlessness” — and her sister Diti is the “bound” one.

domains.title: Boundlessness, Mother of the Ādityas
domains.subtitle: The Unfettered Mother of the Solar Gods
domains.lead: Aditi is the Vedic great mother: the unfettered one, mother of the Ādityas — the solar gods including Mitra, Varuna, and in later count the sun itself. She is space without walls, the cow who yields all plenty, the goddess invoked to loosen every knot that binds a person — sin, sickness, poverty, or a calf bound to its stake.

cards.name: The Unbound
cards.desc: Her name negates “fetter”: she is invoked against every bond — of disease, debt, guilt, or misfortune.

cards.name: Mother of the Ādityas
cards.desc: The solar gods — Mitra, Varuna, Aryaman, and the rest — are her sons, the adityas, “Aditi’s children”.

cards.name: The Cosmic Cow
cards.desc: As the Cow of Plenty she yields milk and freedom; to possess Aditi is to possess space itself.

cards.name: Guardian of Freedom
cards.desc: Her sphere is āditya-freedom: the wideness in which all beings move, breathe, and are pardoned.

mythology.lead: Aditi’s mythology is concentrated in the Veda’s earliest hymns: the mother of the gods whose womb is the sky, whose sons are the days of the year, and to whom the gods themselves owe their radiance. Later tradition reduced her to a genealogy — mother of Vishnu in one Purāṇic strand — but the hymns keep her cosmic: the boundlessness in which everything, including the gods, is contained.

myths.title: The Prayer to Aditi
myths.text: The most famous Aditi-hymn is a prayer for release: ‘May Aditi by whom the gods’ realm is secured, who gives freedom, protect us… Aditi is the sky, Aditi the air, Aditi mother, father, son; Aditi all gods, all men, all that has been and shall be.’ The verse makes her the total container — the theonym for totality itself.

myths.title: The Birth of the Gods
myths.text: The extraordinary theogony-hymn has the gods born of Aditi, and Aditi herself born of Dakṣa, while Dakṣa is born of Aditi — ‘the gods later than the creation’ the poet shrugs, admitting the mystery exceeds the scheme. Aditi here is older than genealogy: the matrix in which the generations turn.

myths.title: Mother of the Days
myths.text: The Ādityas, her sons, are the months and the year — the solar measure. To be born under Aditi is to be born into time’s wideness; the Vedic householder’s morning prayer placed his day under her sons’ jurisdiction and his debts under her power to unbind.

myths.title: Mother of the Dwarf
myths.text: In the Purāṇic revision of the Vāmana myth, Vishnu’s dwarf-incarnation is born to Aditi and Kaśyapa — the mother of boundlessness bearing the god who measures the three worlds in three steps. The pairing compresses her whole theology: from the unmeasured comes the measurer.

lore.syncretism: Aditi is the Vedic prototype of every Hindu great-mother: the later Devī and Lakṣmī inherit her inexhaustibility, and her sons’ names seeded a dozen theophorics. The Avestan opposition of the daeva is absent — in Iran her son Mitra kept his worship as Mithra, while in India the Ādityas were absorbed into Vishnu’s solar theology. Comparative studies pair her with the Greek Eurynome and the Norse Skaði’s freedom-of-the-mountains.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Āditya-names (Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, Dakṣa) seeded the vocabulary of contract, fortune, and skill across the Indo-Iranian world; and the Rigvedic prayer to Aditi is still recited at Indian rites of passage as the formula of release from every bond. ‘Aditi’ survives as a girl’s name across the subcontinent — the boundless given to a daughter.
lore.extendedMeditation: Aditi: the name that means ‘no fetter’. Restored plainly, it is the lexicon’s argument for itself — that names are loosed, not lost, by translation into plain letters. She is the space in which this whole temple stands; the unfettered mother contains the domain.

sources.name: Purāṇic Vāmana cycle (Aditi as Vishnu’s mother)

lore.archaeology: No Aditi temples — her worship was the hymn itself. But the Āditya-lists structured the Vedic ritual’s year, and the solar hymns’ recitation-lists are her monument: a calendar of names kept in the Brahmins’ mouths for three millennia.
lore.cult: Her cult was the morning’s prayer: the Āditya-invocation that loosed the day’s bonds. The Ādityahṛdaya hymn, taught to Rāma in the Rāmāyaṇa before battle, is her tradition’s most famous practical liturgy — the solar mother invoked for victory and unfettered strength.
lore.iconography: Rarely imaged before modernity; the Veda’s image is enough — the cow of plenty, the sky as womb. Modern Indian art renders her as the blue infinite mother with the seven solar children at her feet.
lore.reception: Comparative mythology treats her as the archetype of the ‘unbound mother’ — the theonym that is a philosophical position. Vedic studies cite her 1.89 hymn as the earliest surviving statement of totality-as-goddess; and her name, in modern India, is a blessing parents pronounce daily without knowing they invoke the Rigveda’s oldest sky.
